title: Jade Agent Kit: A Workspace for AI Agents
subtitle: Files, shell, code, search, tools, agents and safe automation in the browser, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: Learn the Jade Agent Kit (version 3), a lean browser workspace for AI agents: the virtual file system, shell, Python, JavaScript and SQLite runtimes, BM25 and vector search, tools for language models, the agent loop and brain, decisions, scheduling, Sentry, notes and safe automation with approvals and secrets. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs that rebuild the ideas.

chapters.title: Meet the kit and lean loading

maps.title: The kit
links: Jade Agent Kit | is | A browser workspace for agents
createKit | creates | The kit with a file system
kit.use | loads | A feature on demand
Lean loading | downloads | Only what you use
Version pin | protects | Your app from changes
Jade Vault | is | Where the pieces come from

summary: The Jade Agent Kit is a workspace that lives inside a web page and gives an AI agent a place to get things done. It has a virtual file system, a shell, Python, JavaScript, SQLite, search, decisions, scheduling and an agent, and every piece is optional.

Its main idea is lean loading. The first call, createKit, sets up only the file system. Each other feature is its own module that downloads the first time a page uses it. A page that needs only files stays tiny.
This course follows the kit's documentation, version 3, and builds small working models of each idea in Python so you understand how the real thing behaves.

glossary.def: The object that createKit returns; every feature hangs off it.
An optional module such as shell, python, sqlite or agent.
Loads one or more features and returns them.
Downloading a feature only when it is first used.
Importing a fixed version so the code never changes under you.
The virtual file system, kit.vfs.

keyPoints: You import createKit from a CDN, pinned to a version such as v3.0.0.
createKit alone loads just the file system (about 6.6 KB gzipped).
kit.use('python') loads Python; kit.use('sqlite', 'bm25') loads several.
Helpers such as kit.run, kit.tool, kit.decide, kit.embed and kit.agent load what they need by themselves.
kit.has('python') tells whether a feature is loaded.
createKit({ use: [...] }) preloads; use: 'all' loads everything.

items: ELI5. The kit is a toolbox you carry in a tiny box. Only the workbench comes with you; the saw and the drill are fetched from the shop the moment a job needs them.

Imagine a toolbox where every tool stays at the shop until you ask for it. That is lean loading. You carry a small box with a workbench in it, the file system, and fetch a saw or a drill only when a job needs one.
The first step is one import from a CDN. You pin the version, because the CDN caches tagged versions permanently and an unpinned import could change your app later.

In this example createKit loads only the file system and keeps it in the browser's IndexedDB under the name my-app. The call to kit.run then loads the shell and its BusyBox program on first use, which is why the output appears after a short wait the first time.

Sizes show the idea. The core is about 6.6 kilobytes gzipped. The shell adds about 12.6 plus 5 kilobytes and a 300 kilobyte WebAssembly file. Python adds 8.5 kilobytes plus about half a megabyte for MicroPython. SQLite adds 9 kilobytes and about 900 kilobytes of WebAssembly.
BM25 search is only 2.1 kilobytes with no extra download.

You can also load features yourself with kit.use, preload them in createKit, or import single modules without createKit at all. Shared code sits in common chunk files so nothing downloads twice, and you can self-host by copying the dist and assets folders together.

chapters.title: The virtual file system

maps.title: VFS
links: kit.vfs | is | An in-memory file system

summary: kit.vfs is a small file system in the browser. Paths look like /notes/a.md. Writing a file creates any missing folders. Because the shell, Python, JavaScript, SQLite, the agent's tools and the brain all use the same file system, a file written by one is seen by all.
By default it lives in memory. With persist set to a name, changes are saved to IndexedDB shortly after each change, and flush saves immediately.
The lab builds a tiny file system to see how paths and folders work.

glossary.def: A slash-separated name such as /logs/run.txt.
Create a folder and any missing parents.
Save to IndexedDB right now.
A copy of the current state.
Load files from an object mapping paths to contents.
Subscribe to changes.

keyPoints: write(path, data) takes a string or bytes and creates missing folders.
read gives a string; readBytes gives a Uint8Array.
list(dir) returns the names in a folder.
exists, isDir and stat inspect a path.
move, copy and rm change the tree.
Data persists only if you set persist; otherwise it is memory only.

items: ELI5. The file system is a pretend filing cabinet inside the web page. Everyone who works in the page, the shell, Python and the agent, opens the same cabinet.

Think of the VFS as a folder tree that exists only inside your web page. It behaves like a normal disk, but nothing touches the user's real files. That makes it a safe place to let an agent write and run things.
Writes create parent folders on their own, so you rarely call mkdirp. The on method lets your page react to changes, for example to redraw a file list when the agent saves a note.
Persistence is a choice. Pass persist with a name when you create the kit and the workspace survives reloads. Leave it out and everything vanishes when the page closes.
The brain, schedules, flows and notes all keep their files under a hidden /.kit folder in this same tree, so persisting the kit persists them too.

Because everything shares the VFS, it is also the meeting point between tools. The agent can write a CSV, Python can read it with open, SQLite can load it, and the shell can count its lines with wc. No copying between systems is needed.

chapters.title: The shell: kit.run and sessions

maps.title: Shell
links: No if or for | means | Use node or python
Engine | can be | auto, wasm or js

summary: kit.run executes a shell command string against the virtual file system. It understands pipes, redirects, and, or, variables, command substitution and globs. The commands come from BusyBox 1.37 compiled to WebAssembly, with JavaScript versions of common ones as a fallback.
A session gives you your own working directory and environment variables, with options for streaming output, a timeout and cancellation. You can also register your own commands as functions.
There are no if or for blocks in the shell. For real scripting, call node or python.

glossary.def: A single program that provides many Unix commands.
Sends one command's output into the next as input.
A shell with its own cwd and env.
Normal output and error output.
0 means success; other numbers mean failure.
A pattern such as *.md that matches file names.

keyPoints: kit.run returns an object with stdout (and the exit status).
A && B runs B only if A succeeds; A || B runs B only if A fails.
kit.shell.session({ cwd, env }) creates a separate shell.
session.run(cmd, { onOutput, timeoutMs, signal }) streams, limits time and can be cancelled.
kit.shell.commands.name = fn registers a custom command.
Built-in extras: node, js, python, python3, sqlite3, sh, xargs, cd, export, which, help.

items: ELI5. The shell is a way to give the computer short written orders. Pipes pass one order's answer to the next, like handing a note down a line of people.

The shell lets an agent do what people do at a terminal: list files, search them, count lines, move things around. Because it is real BusyBox compiled to WebAssembly, the commands behave as you would expect from Linux.

Operators work as in a normal shell. A pipe sends output onward. The && operator runs the next command only if the first succeeded, and || runs it only if the first failed. Variables and command substitution with a dollar sign work too.
There is no if or for in the shell language. This is a deliberate limit: when you need loops or conditions, run a script with node or python, which are available as commands.

A custom command receives a context. It has argv for the arguments, stdin for piped input, o for standard output, e for standard error, and sh.cwd for the working directory. It returns an exit code, and 0 means success.
The engine setting can be auto, wasm or js; auto uses BusyBox when it has loaded.

chapters.title: Python, JavaScript and SQLite

maps.title: Runtimes
links: kit.sqlite | opens | Databases in the VFS

summary: The kit can run code. kit.python runs MicroPython 1.27 in a Web Worker; its open and os see the same virtual file system. kit.js runs JavaScript in another worker with require, fs, path, node:sqlite and fetch, but no npm packages.
kit.sqlite opens database files stored in the VFS and runs SQLite 3.53 in WebAssembly. With sqlite-vec it can store and search vectors, and FTS5 gives full-text search.
In the lab you will build a safe parameterised query.

glossary.def: A small Python for constrained environments.
A background thread in the browser.
Node's way to load a module.
SQL with ? placeholders and values passed separately.
Writes the database back to the VFS.
The sqlite-vec virtual table type.

keyPoints: kit.python.run(code, { cwd }) runs Python; open() and os use the VFS.
kit.js.run(code, { cwd, timeoutMs, globals, network }) returns the script's return value as r.result.
Inside JavaScript, kit.tool(name, args) calls any kit tool.
kit.sqlite.open(path) takes a VFS path or ':memory:'.
db.exec for schema, db.run for writes with params, db.query for rows as objects.
Always pass values as parameters, never glue them into SQL.

items: ELI5. Python and JavaScript are two helpers who can do sums and make decisions. SQLite is a very tidy notebook where facts go in rows you can ask questions about.

Reading and writing files is not enough for most jobs; sometimes the agent needs to compute. The kit offers two languages. Python is handy for data and text. JavaScript is natural in a browser and can use the kit's own tools.

Both run in Web Workers, so a long calculation does not freeze the page, and the timeoutMs option stops runaway code. JavaScript can require fs, path, util, os, http, https and node:sqlite, plus local files, but no packages from npm.

Notice the question marks. A parameterised query keeps the SQL text and the values apart, so a value such as a quote character can never change the meaning of the statement. That is how SQL injection is prevented.
With the sqlite-vec extension a vec0 table stores vectors of a fixed size, and a match query returns the nearest rows with their distance. The next chapters use this for meaning-based search.

chapters.title: BM25 keyword search

maps.title: BM25
links: BM25 | ranks | Documents for a query
Inverse document frequency | rewards | Rare words
BM25 class | builds | A reusable index
searchFiles | searches | Files in a folder

summary: BM25 is a ranking formula for keyword search: documents that contain the query words more often, especially rare words, and that are not too long, score higher. It needs no downloads and is only 2.1 KB in the kit.
kit.bm25.search ranks an array of texts for one query. The BM25 class builds an index once for many queries. searchFiles ranks files under a folder, which is how an agent finds the right note.
The lab implements the scoring yourself.

glossary.def: How many times a word appears in a document.
How many documents contain the word.
Inverse document frequency: rarer words weigh more.
BM25's saturation and length-normalisation parameters.
A prepared structure for quick searching.
The matching line returned by searchFiles.

keyPoints: search(docs, query) returns objects with id, text and score.
new kit.bm25.BM25(docs) builds a reusable index; index.search(query, { limit }).
searchFiles(query, { root }) returns path, score, line and snippet.
Scores are relative: compare them within one search, not across searches.
BM25 matches words, not meaning; embeddings come next.
The page says its scoring follows Python's rank_bm25.

items: ELI5. BM25 is a score for how well a page matches your words: more mentions help, rare words count extra, and a huge page does not win just for being big.

When you search a pile of notes for the word coffee, which note should come first? One that mentions coffee three times is a better guess than one that mentions it once. A note that mentions the rare word espresso is more special than one that only says the common word the.
BM25 turns those instincts into a number.

For each query word, IDF measures how rare it is. The fraction rewards frequent use inside the document, but with diminishing returns controlled by k1, so saying a word ten times is not ten times better. The b term shrinks the score for documents longer than average.

The kit's documentation says its scoring follows the Python library rank_bm25 and does not spell out the constants, so check the source if you need exact numbers. In practice you use the order of results, not the raw scores.

The agent's search_files tool is built on searchFiles. Given a folder, it returns the best matching lines with their file path, which lets an agent find the right place in a big workspace without reading everything.

options: Reduces the score of long documents
quiz.explain: Otherwise long texts would always win.

quiz.explain: It points at the matching line.

practice.title: BM25 score
practice.intro: Write bm25(docs, query): docs is a list of strings, query a string. Lower-case and split on spaces. Use k1=1.5, b=0.75, IDF = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)) where N is the number of docs and n the number containing the word. Return each document's score, rounded to 6 decimals, in the original order. Use import math.
practice.hint: Compute idf per word, then sum per document.
practice.solution:
import math
def bm25(docs, query):
    toks = [d.lower().split() for d in docs]
    N = len(docs)
    avg = sum(len(t) for t in toks) / N
    k1 = 1.5
    b = 0.75
    scores = []
    for t in toks:
        s = 0.0
        for q in query.lower().split():
            n = 0
            for u in toks:
                if q in u:
                    n += 1
            if n == 0:
                continue
            idf = math.log(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5))
            f = t.count(q)
            s += idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(t) / avg))
        scores.append(round(s, 6))
    return scores

chapters.title: Embeddings and vector search

maps.title: Vectors
links: Embedding | is | A vector for text
Hybrid search | merges | Meaning and keywords

summary: An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so that texts with similar meaning have nearby vectors. kit.embed makes them using a model running locally through Ollama, such as embeddinggemma or nomic-embed-text. Ollama Cloud has no embedding models.
kit.vectors keeps embeddings in a SQLite file using sqlite-vec. A search embeds your question and returns the nearest records. Hybrid search also uses BM25 and merges the two rankings.
The labs compute similarity and merge rankings.

glossary.def: A vector that captures meaning.
Closeness of direction of two vectors.
The stored vector closest to the query.
Combining semantic and keyword rankings.
A vector database opened with kit.vectors.open.
Merging rankings by position.

keyPoints: kit.embed(text) gives one vector; kit.embed(array, { model }) gives many.
store = await kit.vectors.open(path); store.add(items); store.search(query, { limit }).
Results have id, text, meta, distance and score.
{ hybrid: true } merges meaning search with BM25.
A store remembers its model and rejects vectors from another.
Pull an embedding model in Ollama first.

items: ELI5. An embedding turns a sentence into a spot on a big map, where sentences that mean the same live close together. Searching is finding the nearest neighbours.

Keyword search fails when the words differ: a note about cats sleeping many hours will not match the question how long do kittens nap. An embedding places both near each other because their meanings are close.
The store embeds each text when you add it and the query when you search. Closeness is usually measured by cosine similarity, which compares direction, not length.
A store records which model made its vectors and refuses vectors from a different model, because numbers from different models cannot be compared.

Meaning search and keyword search each miss things the other finds, so hybrid mode runs both and merges the results. One common way to merge is reciprocal rank fusion: each list gives a document the score one over a constant plus its rank, and the scores are added.
The memory and skills parts of the agent brain can use the same embeddings to find the most relevant facts or skills for each prompt, which is covered in a later chapter.

chapters.title: Tools for language models

maps.title: Tools
links: kit.tools | describes | Tools to a model
kit.tool | runs | A tool by name

summary: A language model cannot touch files or run code by itself. It can only ask for a tool call. kit.tools gives the model a description of each tool, and kit.tool(name, args) runs the call and returns the result as text.

The kit generates definitions in two shapes: the OpenAI shape, which Ollama also uses, and the Anthropic shape. You can add your own tools with a description, a JSON Schema for the inputs and a run function.
The labs build a dispatcher and a schema generator.

glossary.def: A function the model may ask to run.
A standard way to describe the shape of arguments.
Code that runs a tool by name.
The model's request: a name and arguments.
Text returned to the model.
A chosen list of tools to offer.

keyPoints: kit.tools.openai() returns { type: 'function', function: { name, description, parameters } } entries.
kit.tools.anthropic(['read', 'bash']) returns { name, description, input_schema } entries.
kit.tool(name, args) always returns a string; errors begin with 'Error:'.
Built in: read, write, edit, bash, python, javascript, sqlite, search_files, decide, tasks, schedule, sentry, search, fetch.
kit.tools.add(name, { description, parameters, run }) registers a tool.
edit needs oldText to be unique unless replaceAll is set.

items: ELI5. Tools are the things a helper is allowed to ask for, like passing a note through a slot: please read this file. Whatever comes back is always a note of words.

Picture a model as a clever person in a locked room who can pass notes through a slot. The note says: please read this file. You do it and pass the contents back. Tools are the list of requests you are willing to carry out, and the description of each tells the model how to ask.

There are two description shapes because providers differ. In the OpenAI shape every entry says type function and holds the name, a description and a parameters schema. In the Anthropic shape the entry has name, description and input_schema. The content is the same.

The dispatcher kit.tool takes a name and an arguments object and always returns a string. If something goes wrong, the string begins with the word Error and a colon. Checking that prefix is how your code, or the model, notices failure.
Returning text instead of throwing lets the model read the error and try again.
The edit tool shows careful tool design. It replaces exact text, and the old text must appear exactly once unless replaceAll is set. That stops the model from changing the wrong place by accident.

Most of the other built-ins are tools you have already met: python, javascript and sqlite run code, search_files uses BM25, decide asks a decision model, and tasks, schedule and sentry manage lists, jobs and rules. The search and fetch tools use Ollama Cloud and need a cloud key.

chapters.title: The agent loop

maps.title: Agent
links: kit.agent | is | A small coding agent
Six tools | are | read write edit bash search fetch

summary: kit.agent() builds a small coding agent in the style of the pi agent. It pairs a model running on Ollama with a loop and a fixed set of tools: read, write, edit, bash, search and fetch. Ask it to write a file, run it and report, and it does so.

The loop is simple. Send the conversation to the model. If the reply asks for tools, run them and add the results to the conversation, then ask again. When the reply is plain text, the turn is over. maxSteps stops runaway loops.
The lab simulates the loop with a scripted model.

glossary.def: A model plus a loop plus tools.
One prompt and everything the agent does to answer it.
One model call in the loop.
A message sent to onEvent while the agent works.
Where the model runs: cloud or local.
The conversation so far, agent.messages.

keyPoints: Pass ollamaKey to createKit for Ollama Cloud; omit it for Ollama on your machine.
Defaults: gpt-oss:120b on cloud, qwen3:8b locally; maxSteps defaults to 40.
Methods: prompt(text), abort(), reset(), and the messages list.
Events: text, thinking, tool_call, tool_result, turn_end, done, error (and route, context, compaction with a brain).
search and fetch always use Ollama Cloud, so they need a cloud key.
Give extra tools with tools: [...DEFAULT_TOOLS, 'tasks', 'schedule'].

items: ELI5. The agent loop is ask, do, tell, repeat. The model asks for a tool, the kit does it and reports back, and this goes on until the model just answers in words.

The agent is a loop in which a model asks for things and the kit does them. That is all. The surprise is how much a small loop can accomplish when the tools are good, since reading, writing, editing and running a shell cover most of what a programmer does.

Each pass through the loop is a step. The model may stream thinking and text, and it may emit a tool call. The kit runs the tool, produces a tool result, appends it, and calls the model again. When the model answers without asking for a tool, the turn ends and prompt resolves with the answer.

Options let you tune this. The system option sets the instructions. The think option asks supporting models to reason at low, medium or high effort. The tools option picks which tools the model may use. maxSteps, 40 by default, stops a confused agent from looping forever.

Where the model runs is a choice. With a cloud key the default is Ollama Cloud. Without one, the agent uses Ollama on the machine at the default address. The two clients are available as kit.ollama and kit.local, and both offer chat, models, embed, webSearch and webFetch.

Because everything happens in the shared virtual file system, an agent task like write fizzbuzz.py, run it and show me the output is just three tool calls: write, bash, then a final reply. Nothing leaves the browser except the model calls.

chapters.title: The agent brain

maps.title: Brain
links: Router | limits | Which tools are sent

summary: The brain is a set of optional parts you switch on with kit.agent({ brain }). Each part downloads on first use, adds its own tool and hooks into the loop. Their files live as plain text under /.kit/ in the file system, so people can read and edit them.

Memory remembers facts and finds the right ones for each prompt. Skills are instructions the agent loads when needed. The guard keeps long chats inside the model's context window. The router sends only the tools a message seems to need.
Other parts add a knowledge graph with proofs, tree-of-thoughts thinking, sub-agents and chat history.
The labs build a compactor, a secret filter and a tool router.

glossary.def: How much text the model can read at once.
Replacing older turns with a summary.
A folder with a SKILL.md of instructions.
Code that hooks into the agent loop.
A short note written after each prompt.
Chooses tools or models for each prompt.

keyPoints: brain: ['memory', 'skills', 'history', 'guard'] picks parts; brain: true turns on memory, skills, history and guard; 'all' loads everything.
memory keeps /.kit/memory/Memory.md, retrieves by BM25 (or embeddings) and filters out anything that looks like a password or key.
skills reads /.kit/SOUL.md, /AGENTS.md and /.kit/SYSTEM.md, and skills in /.kit/skills/<name>/SKILL.md.
guard estimates request size and compacts older turns near the limit.
router sends core tools and exposes the rest through more_tools.
delegate spawns a read-only sub-agent unless write: true; knowledge proves or contradicts claims; think runs a verified search.

items: ELI5. The brain adds a notebook for remembering, a recipe folder for skills, a backpack that shrinks old chats, and a short list of tools so the helper is not overwhelmed.

A bare agent has a short memory and a big appetite for context. The brain adds the things a long-lived assistant needs, and you choose which. This matches the kit's lean spirit: a part you do not enable costs nothing.

Memory stores facts as plain text under sections. For each new prompt it retrieves the best-matching lines, so the model sees only what is relevant. It refuses to save anything that looks like a password or key.
With the journal option the model writes a short entry after each prompt, and durable facts it names are remembered.

Skills give the agent know-how without bloating every prompt. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md. When there are more than fifteen, only the closest matches are listed. Persona and standing instructions come from SOUL.md and AGENTS.md.
The agent course you are reading is itself built on the idea that instructions can be files.

The guard watches the size of each request. When the chat nears the context window, it compacts older turns into a summary and keeps the latest turns whole. It even learns a model's true limit from prompt is too long errors and retries.
The router saves tokens. Offering forty tools to a model costs context, so it sends the core tools plus those a message seems to need and lets the model ask for more with more_tools.
The knowledge part holds facts and rules and returns proven, contradicted or unknown with a proof, so claims can be checked rather than trusted.

Delegate hands a sub-task to a fresh sub-agent that is read-only by default, limited in steps and time, and returns one report. Think explores several approaches and verifies each by running code, a shell command, a file check or a rubric; a failed hard check removes that branch.

chapters.title: Decisions: fast calibrated choices
summary: Not every question needs a long conversation. kit.decide sends a state, such as a log line or a message, and a question to a small decision model that answers with calibrated probabilities. It is meant for quick, cheap jobs like triage, routing and checks.
There are three kinds. choice picks one of your options. score rates the state on a scale you define. yesno answers a question with a boolean. The result always includes how confident the model is.
The labs reshape probabilities into the kit's result form.

glossary.def: A small model trained to give probabilities for a choice.
Probabilities that match how often the answer is right.
One possible answer.
The probability of the chosen answer.
Sorting items by type or urgency.
Where the decision model runs.

keyPoints: type: 'choice' (default) needs options; the result has result, choice, confidence and probabilities.
type: 'score' rates against your options such as low, medium, high.
type: 'yesno' returns a boolean answer.
kit.decisions picks the server: 'ollaya' (default), 'ollama' (0.35 or later) or 'cloud'.
The kit translates between server formats so answers look the same.
Give an agent the decide tool by adding it to tools.

items: ELI5. A decision model answers quick questions with percentages, like a weather forecast for answers: 91 out of 100 sure it is a bug. If it is unsure, ask a person.

A language model that writes paragraphs is overkill for the question is this log line an error or a warning. A decision model is smaller and answers with numbers: 91 percent bug, 6 percent network, 3 percent user input.
The numbers let you act, for example by asking a person when the confidence is low.

Servers differ in how they take options and report answers. Ollaya takes options as a list and returns a boolean for yes or no. Ollama takes options as an object and derives yes or no from the probability of true. The kit hides these differences so your code sees one shape.

Configure the backend with createKit decide settings or kit.decisions: the server, the model such as winnow:e4b, and optionally host and apiKey. Ollama Cloud needs a cloud key, and its clef model needs a paid plan or credits.

Because the answer includes probabilities, you can build rules like: if confidence is below 70 percent, ask the agent or the user. This pattern, a cheap fast check first and a larger model only when unsure, is a good way to make an agent both quick and careful.

chapters.title: Scheduling and tasks

maps.title: Schedule
links: kit.schedule | runs | Jobs on a timetable
Job kinds | are | command, prompt, js, python, run
Page open | is required | For jobs to run

summary: kit.schedule runs jobs at times you describe in plain English, like every monday at 6pm, or in five-field cron form. A job can run a shell command, a JavaScript or Python snippet, an agent prompt, or a function. kit.tasks keeps a simple task list that people and agents share.

Jobs run only while a page with the kit is open. A job missed while the page was closed runs once when it reopens. Jobs are saved to /.kit/schedule.json, except function jobs, which you re-add on each load.
The labs write a cron matcher and a small task list.

glossary.def: A five-field schedule: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.
A saved action with a when.
A scheduled time that passed while the page was closed.
A to-do with status and optional notes and due date.
Run a job immediately.
A repeat step such as */5.

keyPoints: kit.schedule.add({ name, when, command | prompt | js | python | run }).
when understands 'every day at 2am', 'in 20 minutes', '@hourly' or 5-field cron, in local time.
list(), runNow(name), disable(name), remove(name); on emits run, error, change.
scheduler: false in createKit keeps it stopped until kit.schedule.start().
kit.cron has fromText, parse, next, upcoming and describe.
kit.tasks: add, start, done, update, list, text, on, clear.

items: ELI5. The scheduler is an alarm clock that runs a job instead of ringing. Cron is just the five little boxes that say which minute, hour and day to go off.
A scheduler is an alarm clock that runs code. You describe when in the way you would say it aloud, and the kit turns it into cron, the classic five-field format that Unix has used for decades.

In cron the five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. A star means every value, a number means that value, a comma lists several, a dash gives a range, and a slash gives a step, so star slash five in the minute field means every five minutes.

Everything happens in a web page, so there is no background server. If the user closes the page, nothing runs. When they open it again, a job that was missed runs once to catch up. This is the right trade for a browser tool but means you should not rely on exact timing for critical work.

Tasks give the agent and the user a shared checklist. The agent can add, start and finish tasks through the tasks tool, and your page can show the same list with kit.tasks.on. Give an agent both with tools set to the defaults plus tasks and schedule.

chapters.title: Sentry, notes and senses

maps.title: Sentry
links: Sentry | watches | The page and device
Rule | has | A condition and an action

summary: Sentry is a rule engine that watches the page and the device and acts when a condition occurs. It can watch things like battery, network, idle time, keys, motion, light, location, sound level, camera changes, and your own states and events. Sensitive sources must be allowed by the app.
The kit also includes a notes vault in the style of Obsidian, stored on the file system, with wiki links, backlinks, tags, search, renames that update links, daily notes and templates.
Senses let an agent reach the world: HTTP with secrets, MCP servers, camera, microphone, location, other sensors, and a look tool that lets the agent see an image.

glossary.def: A watch on a source with a condition and an action.
A [[Note name]] reference to another note.
A note that links to this one.
A #word that groups notes.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way to connect tools.
A source that needs the app's permission, like location.

keyPoints: Sentry watches battery, network, idle, keys, motion, light, location, sound level, camera change and custom events.
createKit({ sentry: { allow: ['location'] } }) lets the app permit sensitive systems.
Agents manage rules through the sentry tool.
Notes support [[wiki links]], backlinks, #tags, search, daily notes and templates.
Renaming a note updates every link to it.
look lets the agent see an image; backups can be gzip, optionally encrypted.

items: ELI5. Sentry is a night watchman who looks for things you told him about, like low battery, and then does what you wrote on his list. Notes are linked pages, like a wiki.
Most of the kit waits for you to ask it something. Sentry turns that around: it watches and speaks up. A rule might say when the battery drops below twenty percent, save everything and tell the user.

Sources include the battery, the network state, whether the user is idle, key presses, motion, light level, location, sound level and a change in what the camera sees. You can also define your own states and events so your app can feed rules with its own information.

Some sources are sensitive. The app must permit them through the allow option, so an agent can create a rule about location only when the page owner has said yes. This keeps the power to watch under the human's control.

The notes feature is a personal wiki stored in the file system. A note links to another with double square brackets. The kit can show backlinks, the notes that point to a note, search by text or tag, rename a note and fix every link to it, and make daily notes from a template.

Senses connect the workspace to the outside. HTTP calls can use secrets without exposing them. MCP servers add more tools. Camera, microphone, location and other sensors give the agent input, and the look tool lets it see an image. Backups compress the workspace and can encrypt it.

chapters.title: Automation and staying safe

maps.title: Automation
links: Secrets | stay | Out of the file system
Agents | cannot | Approve their own playbooks

summary: The kit can automate. Flows are n8n-style workflows of steps with triggers. Playbooks are Ansible-style task lists that run without a model. Autonomy keeps a work queue within budgets, a heartbeat checks a list every few minutes, and curiosity makes the agent explore on its own.

Automation needs guard rails. A playbook runs unattended only after your app approves it, and any change needs approval again. Agents can save playbooks but cannot approve them. Secrets such as API keys are passed in by the app, kept out of the file system, and referred to by name only.
This final chapter ties the kit together and ends with a design checklist.

glossary.def: A saved workflow of steps with a trigger.
An approved task list that runs without a model.
A human or app decision required before running.
A limit on steps per hour or per day.
A periodic check of /.kit/HEARTBEAT.md.
A value kept out of files and logs.

keyPoints: Flows: step types include tool, js, shell, decide, llm, agent, file, set, if, switch, each, wait, notify, playbook, flow and stop; triggers are manual, schedule or file change.
Playbooks support when, loop, register, retries, block/rescue/always, assert, tags and secrets redacted from logs.
playbooks.approve(name) or an approve callback in createKit; changes require re-approval.
Autonomy: queue with priorities that age, deadlines, budgets, quiet hours; it pauses while the user is active.
Heartbeat: a reply of HEARTBEAT_OK stays silent; anything else raises an alert.
createKit({ secrets: { NAME: value } }); agents see names and use {{ NAME }}.

items: ELI5. Automation lets the helper work while you are away, but safely: a grown-up must okay each routine first, keys stay in a locked drawer, and there is a limit on how much it may do.
Once an assistant can act, people want it to act on its own: summarise my inbox every evening, check my list every half hour. The kit supports this, and its design shows how to do it carefully.

A flow is a list of steps. Each step does one thing, like read a file, ask a model, or notify the user, and the output of one step is available to the next through double-brace expressions that run in a sandboxed worker. Triggers can be manual, on a schedule, or when a file changes.

A playbook is stricter. It is a list of tasks run without any model in the loop, with conditions, loops, retries and cleanup blocks. Because it runs unattended, it must be approved by your app before its first run, and any edit requires approval again.
An agent may write a playbook, but cannot approve it. That separation is the central safety idea.

Autonomy lets the agent work through a queue by itself, but within budgets of steps per hour and per day, outside quiet hours, and pausing while the user is active. Tools on a deny list wait for an explicit allow.
The heartbeat is the gentlest form: every N minutes the agent reads a checklist and replies HEARTBEAT_OK if nothing needs attention, which stays silent.

Secrets are handled by name. The app hands API keys to the kit, which keeps them out of the file system and redacts them from logs. The agent sees only names and writes {{ NAME }} where the value is needed, so a prompt injection cannot make it print a key it never saw.

A design checklist to finish. Start lean and load only what you use. Persist the kit if work must survive. Give the agent only the tools it needs. Make the human the approver for anything unattended. Keep secrets out of files. Allow sensitive senses deliberately.
Prefer many small, checked steps to one large leap.
